title: Kinematics (suvat)
goals: Name the five suvat quantities and pick the equation that fits what you know
Work out speeds, times and distances for constant acceleration
Work out a stopping distance, and say why doubling the speed quadruples it
Read acceleration and distance from a velocity–time graph
Work out how long something takes to fall from a height
summary:
**Kinematics** describes motion without asking what causes it. For motion in a straight line with **constant acceleration**, five quantities, **suvat**:

- $s$ displacement (m): how far, in a stated direction
- $u$ initial velocity (m/s)
- $v$ final velocity (m/s)
- $a$ acceleration (m/s²): how much the velocity changes each second
- $t$ time (s)

The equations, each missing one quantity:

- $v = u + at$ (no $s$)
- $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ (no $v$)
- $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$ (no $a$)
- $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ (no $t$)

**Method**: write down the three you know and the one you want; choose the equation without the fifth.

Slowing down is a **negative** acceleration (a deceleration). Stopping from speed $u$ at deceleration $a$: $s = \frac{u^2}{2a}$. Speed is **squared**: twice the speed, four times the stopping distance.

**Velocity–time graph**: the **gradient** (steepness) is the acceleration; the **area** under it is the displacement.

**Free fall**: with no air resistance, everything accelerates down at $g = 9.81$ m/s². Dropped from height $h$: $t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}$.

Pick a positive direction and stick to it: velocities and accelerations the other way are negative.

formulas.name: Velocity after a time
formulas.says: Start speed plus how much it gains each second, times the seconds.
formulas.example: From 3 m/s at 2 m/s² for 4 s: 11 m/s.

formulas.name: Displacement from time
formulas.says: The distance at the start speed, plus the extra from speeding up.
formulas.example: From rest at 2 m/s² for 5 s: $0 + 0.5 \times 2 \times 25 = 25$ m.

formulas.name: Displacement from the average velocity
formulas.says: With steady acceleration, the average velocity is halfway between the start and end, and distance is average velocity × time.
formulas.example: From 4 to 10 m/s in 3 s: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 14 \times 3 = 21$ m.

formulas.name: Velocity and displacement, no time
formulas.says: Links the speeds to the distance without the time.
formulas.example: Stopping from 20 m/s at 5 m/s²: $0 = 400 - 10s$, $s = 40$ m.

bench.task: Time a conveyor's or a lift's start: with a stopwatch, its final speed (from the drive's display or a known belt speed) and the ramp time on the drive, work out the acceleration and the distance used to get up to speed. Watch from a safe place: no guards opened.
check: Read the final speed and the acceleration ramp time
Does it match how far the load moved before running steadily?

cards.q: A forklift brakes to a stop from 2 m/s in 0.8 m. Braking the same way from 4 m/s, how far does it take?
cards.why: Stopping distance goes with speed squared ($s = \frac{u^2}{2a}$): twice the speed, four times the distance: $4 \times 0.8 = 3.2$ m. Doubling to 1.6 m is the usual guess, and the dangerous one.

cards.title: Five quantities
cards.body:
For straight-line motion with **constant acceleration**, five quantities describe everything:

- $s$: **displacement**, in metres, in a stated direction
- $u$: the velocity at the **start**, m/s
- $v$: the velocity at the **end**, m/s
- $a$: the **acceleration**, m/s²: how much the velocity changes each second
- $t$: the **time**, s

Know any three and you can find the other two. Choose a positive direction; anything the other way is negative.
cards.more:
m/s² reads 'metres per second, per second': an acceleration of 2 m/s² means the speed goes up by 2 m/s every second: 0, 2, 4, 6 m/s…

Velocity has a direction; speed does not. A ball thrown up at 10 m/s has $u = +10$ (up positive) and $a = -9.81$ (gravity pulls down).

The 'constant acceleration' matters: these equations are wrong for a car pulling away hard then easing off. Real moves are often split into parts that are each close to constant: speed up, cruise, slow down (the motion profiles lesson does exactly that).

cards.q: Match each letter with what it stands for.

cards.title: Velocity after a time: v = u + at
cards.body:
Each second the velocity changes by $a$. After $t$ seconds it has changed by $at$:

$$v = u + at$$

Rearranged for the time to reach a speed: $t = \frac{v - u}{a}$; for the acceleration: $a = \frac{v - u}{t}$.
cards.more:
Numbers: a trolley at 3 m/s accelerates at 2 m/s² for 4 s. Each second it gains 2 m/s; in 4 s, 8 m/s. So $v = 3 + 8 = 11$ m/s.

A drive's acceleration ramp works the same way. A conveyor ramped from 0 to 1.5 m/s in 3 s has $a = \frac{1.5 - 0}{3} = 0.5$ m/s².

Slowing down: $a$ is negative. From 12 m/s at −3 m/s², after 2 s: $12 - 6 = 6$ m/s.

cards.q: A trolley starts at {u} m/s and accelerates at {a} m/s² for {t} s. How fast is it going then?
cards.why: It gains {a} m/s every second for {t} s, on top of its starting {u} m/s.

cards.title: How far: two ways
cards.body:
With steady acceleration, the **average** velocity is halfway between the start and end, so

$$s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$$

If you do not know $v$, use

$$s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$$

$ut$ is how far it would go at the start speed; $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ is the extra from speeding up.
cards.more:
Numbers: from 4 to 10 m/s in 3 s. The average is 7 m/s; in 3 s that is 21 m. Same answer from the other equation: $a = 2$, so $4 \times 3 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 9 = 12 + 9 = 21$ m.

Where does the half come from? On a speed–time graph the extra speed builds up as a triangle: its area is half the base (t) times the height (at): $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$.

From rest, $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$: distance grows with time squared. In twice the time it goes four times as far.

cards.q: A trolley starts at {u} m/s and accelerates at {a} m/s² for {t} s. How far does it go?
cards.why: The start speed's distance plus the extra from accelerating. Forgetting to square the time is the usual slip.

cards.title: No time given: v² = u² + 2as
cards.body:
When the time is neither known nor wanted:

$$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$

Its most useful form is the **stopping distance**: braking to $v = 0$ from $u$ at a deceleration $a$:

$$s = \frac{u^2}{2a}$$

The speed is **squared**: twice the speed, **four times** the distance. That is why speed limits near people are so low.
cards.more:
Numbers: 20 m/s (about 45 mph) braking at 5 m/s²: $\frac{400}{10} = 40$ m. At 40 m/s: $\frac{1600}{10} = 160$ m.

On a machine: an axis moving at 0.5 m/s that can decelerate at 2 m/s² needs $\frac{0.25}{4} = 0.0625$ m, about 63 mm, to stop. So a hard limit switch must sit at least that far before the end stop, plus the time for the system to react.

That reaction time adds a distance at full speed too ($u \times$ reaction time), as in the Highway Code's thinking plus braking distance.

cards.q: A vehicle at {u} m/s brakes at a steady {a} m/s². How far does it travel before it stops?
cards.why: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ with $v = 0$ and a deceleration of {a}: $s = \frac{u^2}{2a}$.
cards.hint: Final velocity 0; the time is not needed.

cards.title: Choosing the equation
cards.body:
1. Write down **s, u, v, a, t**.
2. Fill in the three you know; mark the one you want.
3. The fifth is the one you neither know nor want: use the equation **without** it.

No $s$: $v = u + at$; no $v$: $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$; no $a$: $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$; no $t$: $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$.

Watch the hidden values: 'from rest' means $u = 0$; 'comes to a stop' means $v = 0$; 'dropped' means $u = 0$ and $a = g$.
cards.more:
Example: a lift accelerates from rest to 2 m/s over 3 m. How long does that take?

s = 3, u = 0, v = 2, a = ?, t = wanted. The one not known or wanted is $a$, so use the equation without $a$: $s = \tfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$. $3 = \tfrac{1}{2}(0 + 2)t$, so $t = 3$ s.

You could find $a$ first and then $t$, but two steps means two chances to slip.

cards.q: A cart goes from 2 m/s to 8 m/s over 15 m. You want the acceleration. Which equation?
cards.why: Known: u, v, s; wanted: a; not involved: t. The equation without t is $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$: $64 = 4 + 30a$, so $a = 2$ m/s².

cards.title: Velocity–time graphs
cards.body:
Plot velocity up, time across:

- the **gradient** (rise ÷ run) is the **acceleration**: a straight line means constant acceleration; flat means steady speed
- the **area** under the line is the **displacement**

A move that speeds up, cruises and slows down is a **trapezium**: area = $\tfrac{1}{2}$(the two parallel sides added) × the height, or split it into triangles and a rectangle.
cards.more:
Why area? At a steady 5 m/s for 4 s you go 20 m: that is the rectangle 5 high and 4 wide. When the speed changes, the area still adds up all the little bits of speed × time.

Numbers: a conveyor speeds up from 0 to 1 m/s in 2 s, runs at 1 m/s for 6 s, slows to 0 in 2 s. Areas: triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 1 = 1$, rectangle $6 \times 1 = 6$, triangle 1. Total 8 m.

The motion profiles lesson used this in mm and mm/s for servo moves; the maths is the same.

cards.q: A move speeds up from rest to {v} m/s in {t1} s, runs at {v} m/s for {t2} s, then slows to rest in {t1} s. How far does it go?
cards.why: The area under the velocity–time graph is the distance. The two ramps are triangles (half base × height each); the cruise is a rectangle.
cards.hint: Split the trapezium into two triangles and a rectangle.

cards.q: A van at 18 m/s brakes at 6 m/s² to a stop. How long does it take, and how far does it go?

steps.ask: The distance (no t needed, to avoid reusing a worked value).

steps.show: Average $\tfrac{1}{2}(18 + 0) = 9$ m/s for 3 s is 27 m. ✓

cards.why: List suvat, pick each equation by what it leaves out, and check one answer another way. Deceleration goes in as negative.

cards.q: Why does step 1 write the acceleration as −6, not 6?
cards.context: u = 18 m/s forward, braking at 6 m/s².
cards.model: The positive direction was chosen as the way the van is moving, so its starting velocity is +18. Braking makes the velocity smaller, so the acceleration points the other way: negative. With +6 the equations would describe the van speeding up, and v = u + at would never reach zero.
points: Braking acts against it, so a is negative
With +6 the van would speed up instead

cards.q: A spanner is dropped from a platform 5 m up. How long does it take to land, and how fast is it going? (Ignore air resistance; g = 9.81 m/s².)
cards.why: 'Dropped' gives $u = 0$; gravity gives $a$. About 10 m/s after a 5 m fall: why hard hats and toe boards matter.

cards.q: A bolt is dropped from {h} m up. How long does it take to reach the ground? (g = 9.81 m/s², no air resistance.)
Distance covered from rest at 3 m/s² in 4 s. One line is wrong. Which?
cards.why: The time is squared. Check with the average speed: it ends at 12 m/s, so averages 6 m/s over 4 s: 24 m.

cards.q: A belt speeds up steadily from {u} m/s to {v} m/s in {t} s. How far does a point on it travel meanwhile?
cards.why: Steady acceleration: the average velocity is halfway between start and end; times the time.

cards.q: A cart goes from {u} m/s to {v} m/s over {s} m. What is its acceleration?
cards.why: No time involved, so $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$, rearranged for $a$.

cards.q: On a velocity–time graph, what does a flat (horizontal) line show?
cards.why: The gradient is the acceleration; flat means zero. It is standing still only if that flat line is at zero velocity.

cards.q: A servo axis accelerates from rest at {a} mm/s² to {v} mm/s. How far does it travel while accelerating, in mm?
cards.why: Same suvat, in mm and mm/s: $v^2 = 2as$ from rest. The motion profiles lesson calls it $d_{acc} = \frac{v^2}{2a}$.

cards.q: A drive ramps a conveyor from rest to {v} m/s with an acceleration of {a} m/s². How long is the ramp?
cards.why: $v = u + at$ rearranged: time = change in velocity ÷ acceleration. No distance needed here.

cards.q: From rest, with the same acceleration, how much further does something travel in 6 s than in 3 s?
cards.why: From rest, $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$: distance goes with time squared, so twice the time is four times the distance.

cards.q: A car's stopping distance at 30 mph is 14 m (braking only). At 60 mph, braking the same way, it is about…
cards.why: Braking distance goes with speed squared: twice the speed, four times the distance.

cards.q: From {u} m/s at {a} m/s² for {t} s. Final velocity?
Stopping from {u} m/s at {a} m/s². Distance?
